label: paragraph_title
text: COMMERCE AND FINANCE

label: paragraph_title
text: DODGE BROTHERS

label: paragraph_title
text: GIGANTIC MOTOR BUSINESS.

label: text
text: Brotherly love builded a gigantic organization for John F. and Horace E. Dodge, founders of Dodge Brothers, Inc., which has just been sold to a syndicate of bankers.

label: text
text: Both were reared at Niles, Mich., and from earliest boyhood these brothers remained inseparable. From that day in Niles when in their father's machine shop they constructed the first bicycle ever seen in their home town, until both passed on in 1920, the brothers were the closest of chums and business associates.

label: text
text: They came to Detroit in the early 18th century, eighties and struggled through years of poverty. First they worked in a boiler factory; then they entered the employ of the Canadian Typograph Company at Windsor, Ont., and from this competition was born Dodge Brothers, Inc. For two years they manufactured the Evan and Dodge bicycle. In 1901 they opened a machine shop in Detroit, employing 12 hands.

label: text
text: Nineteen years later, more than 18,000 men were employed here.

label: text
text: The first Dodge factory was built in 1910, and became the nucleus of the mammoth auto-mobile plant involved in the present sale.

label: text
text: The first contract of Dodge Brothers in the automobile world came in 1902, and there followed years in which the Dodges manufactured many of the parts for the Ford Motor Company, and the brothers came into possession of a large block of Ford Motor Company stock. In the summer of 1910 they sold their Ford holdings to Hepry and Edset Ford for nearly $25,000,000. During the interim the stock had netted millions in dividends.

label: text
text: Until the last France was the plant superintendent and manufacturer and John the business head.

label: text
text: Horace "Dodge's" estate was appraised at $37,186,588 and that of John "Dodge" at $36,942,727. In Dodge Brothers, Inc., each brother held 50 per cent. of the stock.

label: paragraph_title
text: AUSTRIAN RAILWAYS

label: paragraph_title
text: ELECTRIFICATION MAKING PROGRESS.

label: text
text: From Prague word "comes of definite plans on which the Government of Czechoslovakia is engaged for the electrification this year of the railway from Pilsen to the capital, and it is also understood that it will not be" long before only electrically-driven locomotives are employed within the city limits, thus avoiding the smoke to which the districts near the railway lines and the stations are subjected.

label: text
text: From the third of these Central European countries, Hungary, the news is entirely encouraging. The Pester Lloyd of Budapest reported recently that a British firm is about to erect a water-power works at Varpolata, which would supply 100,000 horsepower. This would be sufficient for the needs of Budapest and would be used as well for the electrification of the railway line from this city to Bruck and, on the other side of the Danube River, as far as Balaton. Other electrification projects are also under consideration by an American firm.

label: paragraph_title
text: MOTOR ENTERPRISE IN AUSTRALIA.

label: text
text: Mr. P. W. Grandjean, secretary of the Ford Motor Company of Canada, has given the first definite account of the company's Australian plans.

label: text
text: According to this, it has been decided to form two companies, each with a capital of £1,500,000, and both having headquarters at Geelong, 40 miles from Melbourne. A site of 100 acres has been secured.

label: text
text: The Canadian Ford interests will supply the capital required at present, but the directors include Sir Arthur Robinson, member of the Legislative Council of Victoria and a former Solicitor-General, as well as other Australians.

label: text
text: The erection of the assembling and body-building factory will be expedited.

label: text
text: Mr. Grandjean has withheld estimates as to the manufacturing capacity of the new company, but he states that the Ford sales in Australia are now approximately 20,000 cars annually.

label: paragraph_title
text: UGANDA COTTON.

label: paragraph_title
text: NEW EMPIRE SOURCE. //

label: text
text: An African Press correspondent writes: “Possibly the world over there is no other country which has shown such remarkable progress at any time in its history as that which Uganda can show in the matter of cotton growing.”

label: text
text: Taking his figures from conservative official sources he says that the land available for growing good quality cotton may be put down at about 2,000,000 acres. As in 1924 only some 578,000 acres were under cotton, some idea of the vast potentialities of the Province may be gained.

label: text
text: The official estimate of Uganda's cotton yield is put at half a million bales yearly, but experts say that this can be considerably increased, and a case is quoted of a planter who tried the experiment of a catcherop of cotton between his rows of young coffee and averaged 500 pounds to the acre.

label: text
text: The history of cotton-growing in Uganda is an interesting one when looked at in a table of figures. In 1914 a crop of 180 cwts, valued at £236 was exported. Ten years later nearly 120,000 acres were under cotton and the export was 117,000 cwts. valued at over £350,000. The war years kept the yield down, but the 1012 months of 1924 showed 578,114 acres with a yield of 453,750 cwts. of a value of £3,449,223. And cotton averages over 75 per cent. of the total Uganda exports. So it is intelligible that this colony comes easily first among the new cotton-pied-ducing fields of the Empire.

label: text
text: It is satisfactory, too, to learn that cotton-growing is entirely a native industry, worked by many thousands of small cultivators. From trials made with various seed from all parts of the world, two American long-stapled upland varieties were retained—Allen and Sunflower—which have now become established as Uganda cotton. Seed for planting is distributed by the Government's free of charge. The whole of the crop is ginned in the country, the average crop for the last four years representing 90,000,000 lbs. of seed cotton. Formerly it was always sent to Kenya to be ginned and bailed.

label: text
text: Lack of adequate transport facilities is Uganda's chief drawback and one result of this is that thousands of tons of cotton seed are burnt annually up-country. What is exported goes almost entirely to Liverpool for crushing purposes. Growers have come to realize that, until the railways come nearer to them they will have to rely on motor transport to get their produce to the nearest rail point. Over 100 ginneries are now established in different parts of the country, so that the cotton travels down country properly baled.

label: text
text: How vital an industry cotton growing has become to Uganda may be judged from the statistics, which show that the indirect revenue from it is probably twice as much as the direct revenue. Exact figures are not obtainable, as the industry at present is a purely native peasant one.

label: paragraph_title
text: AMERICAN INDUSTRY

label: text
text: Evidently Charles M. Schwab is not to be numbered amongst those who claim that they see no good on the horizon of the near-by future, for he declared before the New York Building Congress the other day that he believed the next twenty years would see the greatest expansion and the greatest accomplishment American industry had ever known. "If I had my choice to be born again, I believe I would choose to be a young man to day," he said. And then he spoke of co-operation between competitors in industry and democratic relations between employer and workingmen. When it comes to be commonly recognized that co-operation is the avenue leading to true success, and that democratic relations between employer and employee constitute without a doubt the key to the business relations of the future, it may be understood why Mr. Schwab has never had a strike among his men.

label: paragraph_title
text: WHEAT

label: text
text: "The production of Garnet wheat may possibly in the near future replace the famous Marquis wheat," L. H. Newman, Dominion Cerealist, Experimental Farms, told the Agricultural Committee of the House of Commons recently. Its capabilities of high production in seasons of drought and to ripen earlier than the Marquis, even in wet weather; thereby escaping the possibilities of rust and frost, are valuable factors in its favour. It was hoped that the growing of Garnet wheat would extend the wheat-growing area many miles further north.

label: paragraph_title
text: BOLD FINANCE PLEA

label: text
text: A CURE FOR UNEMPLOYMENT:

label: text
text: Sir Alfred Mood, speaking at Reading replied to the speech made by the Secretary for War.

label: text
text: Army Estimates, he said, were £6,000,000 in excess of last year. There was not a financier or economist who was not perfectly well aware that the crushing burden of taxation was a dangerous weakness in our industrial and economic life.

label: text
text: Unemployment used to be regarded as temporary and passing, but it had become almost ingrained as permanent and static.

label: text
text: "I am not so afraid as some are of a bold use of our national finance," said Sir Alfred. "I am unconvinced that this country dare not do what other countries are doing—that is, to equip itself in every possible way to the highest degree of efficiency by the expenditure if necessary of national credit. (Cheers.)"

label: text
text: "Let us marry our national credit and our unemployment. Let us not turn down schemes, because the Treasury officials cannot see any immediate return."

label: paragraph_title

label: paragraph_title
text: RISE OF £1,876,000 IN POST OFFICE TOTAL

label: text
text: Estimates for the Revenue Departments for the coming financial year, issued, show a net total of £64,348,635, an increase of £2,046,731.

label: text
text: This is principally due to a rise of £1,876,330 in the Post Office Estimate.

label: text
text: Post Office salaries and allowances have risen by £439,115 to £30,676,065, half the increase being due to metropolitan establishments.

label: text
text: Wireless broadcasting is set down at £350,000, an increase of £50,000.

text: ARMOUR SHARE OFFER.

label: text
text:
Converting dollars at five to the £, the net profits of Armour and Company, the big American meat packing business, amounted to £3,661,947 for 1924, against £2,754,405 for the preceding year.
The offer of 7 per cent. Preferred stock of Armour and Company of Delaware to the company's customers in this country accompanies the accounts for the next year.

label: text
text: The new shares will be sold at the "market price on the Chicago Stock Exchange" on the day of acceptance. The present price is around 92 dollars.

label: text

label: paragraph_title
text: FUR SALE.

label: text
text: The annual spring fur auction sale of the Montreal Fur Auction Sales Company took place in Montreal recently, with an extensive offering of furs with an estimated value of $2,500,000. The furs for auction were gathered from all parts of the world, including India, Africa and Russia. The majority, however, were collected in Canada. There were approximately 500 buyers from New York, Montreal, London, Paris and other fur centres at the sale.

label: text
text: Earl Russell called attention in

label: text
text: the House of Lords to the un. businesslike procedure of the Post Office, and asked for a Departmental Committee of business men.

text: One of his illustrations was the loss of a registered packet; containing £10, addressed to Germany.

label: text
text: A publisher had complained recently of losing eight copies of books sent out for review. Several sent to addresses in the London area took over a week for delivery.

label: text
